title.en: Arjuna on Mount Indrakila: The Ascetic Warrior
title.zh: 阿周那苦修於因陀羅吉拉山

region.en: Mount Indrakila (symbolic pin, East Javanese court geography)
region.zh: 因陀羅吉拉山（象徵性定位，東爪哇宮廷地理）

texts.period: Kakawin Arjunawiwaha composed by Mpu Kanwa, c. 1030 CE, court of Airlangga

source.work: Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha (c. 1030 CE), cantos 1-3 (the tapa)

summary.en: The Arjunawiwaha ('Arjuna's Wedding'), the first great Javanese court epic, opens with the gods in terror: the demon-king Niwatakawaca cannot be conquered until a mortal ascetic's power is ripened. Arjuna, resting between wars, is sent to Mount Indrakila to perform tapa — standing on one leg, taking only wind for food — until the fire of his asceticism endangers the world itself and the gods must send messengers to cool him.
summary.zh: 《阿周那婚禮》——爪哇首部偉大宮廷史詩——開篇即諸神惶恐：魔王尼瓦塔卡瓦查不可克，除非一位凡人苦修者之力臻於圓熟。阿周那於戰暇奉命赴因陀羅吉拉山行『塔帕』苦修——獨腿而立、僅以風為食——直至其苦修之火危及世界，諸神不得不遣使為其降溫。

sensitivity.note: Court kakawin (c. 1030 CE); composed for King Airlangga, read as his mirror. Paraphrase of the kakawin narrative.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the kakawin narrative as summarized in standard editions; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Arjunawiwaha, composed by Mpu Kanwa around 1030 CE for the court of King Airlangga, is the earliest fully surviving Javanese court kakawin, and it opens not with a battle but with a theology of power.

BEGINNING: THE GODS' TERROR. The demon-king Niwatakawaca of Mount Mamertha has accumulated such tapa-power that no god can harm him; the gods' counselor (Indra) perceives that only a human ascetic, ripened by austerity, can match him — and only one mortal is worthy: Arjuna, the Pandawa archer, who has retired between wars. A divine mission descends to ask Arjuna to become, for the moment, a hermit.

MIDDLE: THE TAPA. On Mount Indrakila Arjuna performs the full ascetic discipline: hair matted, body smeared, standing on the tips of his toes, eating nothing but wind, until his radiance scorches the worlds. The gods, alarmed that their own instrument may burn the cosmos, send first the apsaras to tempt him back into flesh and then Indra himself to test his resolve with a hunting-deity disguise and an assault of illusions; Arjuna, unmoved in both temptations, is recognized as a genuine master of desire.

END: THE MISSION ASSIGNED. Pleased, the gods grant Arjuna boons of weapons, and Indra assigns him the conquest of Niwatakawaca — with the crucial counsel that the demon's single vulnerability (his heart hidden beneath his false magic) can be learned only from within the demon's palace, by a woman planted at his side. The war of the kakawin is thus won before it is fought: the hero's ascetic power is to be spent through seduction and information rather than arrows.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative (1) teaches that royal power in Java is founded on tapa (ascetic heat), the same force demons use, held under discipline; (2) models the courtier-king (Airlangga) as Arjuna — powerful, controlled, victorious through wisdom and alliance rather than raw force; (3) supplies the comparative tapa-motif (heat versus heaven) parallel to the Indian sources it adapts; and (4) anchors the whole Javanese tradition of reading epic as statecraft. The choice of Arjuna for the role is itself the kakawin's argument: the archer who has already renounced the rewards of victory in the Indian epic is here sent back into asceticism at the height of his powers, so that the poem can insist that discipline is not the refuge of the weak but the completion of strength. The Indrakila episode also fixes the kakawin's characteristic balance of Sanskrit inheritance and Javanese courtliness: the demon-king plot, the nymphs' temptation and the boons of weapons are recognizably Indian, but the temper of the telling — the emphasis on ceremony, self-command and intelligence as the marks of the victor — is the court of Airlangga looking into the epic as into a mirror. Read this way, the tapa is the poem's training manual for kings: the sovereign who cannot burn the world with his own heat has not yet earned the right to aim it at an enemy.
narrative.zh: 《阿周那婚禮》由坎瓦於約1030年為艾爾朗加之朝所作，為現存最早爪哇宮廷頌詩。其開篇乃權力神學：魔王尼瓦塔卡瓦查苦修之力無神能敵；唯凡人苦修之熱方可相抗——而唯一配得上者，即戰暇退隱之神射手阿周那。他奉神命赴因陀羅吉拉山行塔帕：立於足尖、以風為食，其光芒竟灼燒世界；諸神先遣天女誘惑、後由因陀羅親試幻象，阿周那不動如山，遂被認可為欲望之真主。神乃賜其神兵，授以討魔之命，並授密策：魔王唯一弱點唯有潛入其宮、由枕邊女子探得。功能：立『王室之力源於苦修』之爪哇神學、以艾爾朗加為阿周那之鏡像、提供跨文化之苦修母題、並奠定爪哇『史詩即政術』之解經傳統。

functions: Teaches that royal and demonic power alike flow from tapa (ascetic heat) held under discipline
Models the courtier-king Airlangga as Arjuna: controlled, wise, victorious through alliance
Supplies the Javanese tapa-versus-heaven motif parallel to its Indian sources
Anchors the Javanese tradition of reading epic as statecraft

variants.name: Indian Mahabharata parallel (Kairata episode)
variants.summary: Arjuna's tapa and the contest with Shiva; the Javanese kakawin redirects the power toward the demon-king plot and the heavenly bride.

variants.name: Later wayang lakon of Arjuna's tapa
variants.summary: The tapa becomes a standard wayang play in which Semar and the Punakawan accompany the ascetic, adding comic counterpoint.

primary_sources.citation: Composed c. 1030 CE at the court of Airlangga, Kahuripan, East Java; surviving in Old Javanese MSS (e.g. Leiden cod. or.); narrative paraphrased.

secondary_sources.work: P. J. Zoetmulder, Kalangwan: A Survey of Old Javanese Literature
secondary_sources.citation: Zoetmulder 1974, The Hague: Nijhoff — the standard survey of the kakawin and its court context.

passages.text: The gods are in terror: Niwatakawaca's accumulated austerity makes him invulnerable to every divine weapon, and only the perfected tapa of a mortal can balance him. The divine mission descends to Arjuna, the archer resting between wars, and asks him to become a hermit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (c. 1030), opening cantos; not verbatim.

passages.text: On Mount Indrakila Arjuna stands on the tips of his toes, eats only wind, and lets his radiance scorch the worlds; when the apsaras fail to move him and Indra's disguises fail to break him, the gods recognize a true master of desire and grant him the mission and the boons of weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha; not verbatim.

title.en: The Heavenly Nymphs Failing at the Hermit's Stone

region.zh: 因陀羅吉拉山（象徵性定位）

source.work: Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha (c. 1030 CE), the temptation cantos

summary.en: The most erotic cantos of Old Javanese poetry are sent as a weapon: Indra dispatches the apsara-host — Supraba among them — to melt the hermit's discipline with dance, scent and art. The nymphs tire, dawn finds them defeated, and Arjuna stands 'like a stone' — the kakawin's celebrated paradox that desire fails where it is most beautifully deployed.
summary.zh: 古爪哇詩最香艷的段落被用作武器：因陀羅遣天女之群——蘇普拉巴在其中——以舞、香與藝融解修士之戒律。天女力竭，黎明見其敗退；阿周那立如頑石——爪哇頌詩最著名的悖論：慾望以最美的方式發動，卻在不動者面前失敗。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase; court-erotic imagery treated as literary theology.

passages.text: Indra sends the apsaras of heaven to the hermitage, Supraba first among them; for a night they dance, play, and pour out every art of attraction at the stone-still ascetic. At dawn the nymphs withdraw defeated, and the gods' counselor marvels: the warrior unmoved by the host of heaven's beauty is ripe to be heaven's own weapon. Arjuna is awarded the mission the temptation was meant to disqualify him from.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (c. 1030), temptation cantos; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha; not verbatim.

title.en: Arjuna's Wedding: Supraba Given to the Victor
title.zh: 阿周那婚禮：天女蘇普拉巴歸於勝者

region.zh: 天堂與瑪默爾塔山（象徵性定位）

source.work: Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha (c. 1030 CE), the wedding cantos

summary.en: The kakawin closes with its title-scene: Arjuna, having destroyed Niwatakawaca with Supraba's intelligence, is received in heaven and married to the apsara who was first his enemy's companion and then his co-conspirator — the 'wedding' (iwaha) that seals the alliance of mortal discipline and divine grace.
summary.zh: 頌詩以其題名之場收束：阿周那依蘇普拉巴之智誅滅尼瓦塔卡瓦查，天界迎之，娶那位曾為敵之伴、後為其同謀的天女——這場『婚禮』封印了凡人苦修與神恩的聯盟。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase; read at court as the union of king and divine power.

passages.text: With the demon-king destroyed, Arjuna is welcomed into heaven; Supraba, who had entered the enemy's palace to learn his secret and gave it to the hero, is now given to him as bride. The Arjunawiwaha ends in festival: the marriage of the disciplined mortal and the apsara of heaven, celebrated in the poem's most courtly verse, sealing the theology that the king's power is married, not stolen, from the divine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (c. 1030), wedding cantos; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha; not verbatim.

title.en: Niwatakawaca's Secret: The Demon-King Undone from Within
title.zh: 尼瓦塔卡瓦查之秘：自內而潰的魔王

region.en: Mount Mamertha (symbolic pin, Old Javanese epic geography)
region.zh: 瑪默爾塔山（象徵性定位，古爪哇史詩地理）

source.work: Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha (c. 1030 CE), Niwatakawaca cantos

summary.en: The demon-king Niwatakawaca's invulnerability hides a single mortal secret. Supraba, sent as a bride into his palace, learns it from him and passes it to Arjuna; the hidden heart is struck, and the tapa-armoured tyrant falls — the Javanese epic's doctrine that no citadel of power lacks an inside.
summary.zh: 魔王尼瓦塔卡瓦查刀槍不入，唯藏一致命之秘。蘇普拉巴以新娘之身入其宮，探得其秘而傳於阿周那；隱藏之心被擊中，以苦修為甲的暴君隨之倒下——爪哇史詩之教義：任何權力堡壘皆有內隙。

passages.text: Niwatakawaca, the tapa-powered tyrant of the demons, is armoured against every weapon of the gods; his single vulnerability is hidden where no assault can reach — inside his own palace, in his own confidence. Supraba, sent into the palace as a bride, learns the secret at its source and passes it to Arjuna; the hidden centre is struck and the invulnerable king falls. The epic concludes that power is conquered by knowledge carried in trust, not by force alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (c. 1030); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha; not verbatim.

title.en: The Burning of Smara: The Love-God's Ashes

region.zh: 東爪哇諫義里（創作宮廷）

texts.period: Kakawin Smaradahana composed by Mpu Dharmaja, c. 12th century CE, for King Kamesvara of Kediri

source.work: Kakawin Smaradahana (c. 12th c. CE), the burning of Kama

summary.en: Old Javanese poetry's most poignant catastrophe: to break Shiva's meditation, the love-god Smara (Kama) fires his flower-arrow; the angered god opens his third eye and burns Smara to ash, and desire itself dies from the world. In the poem's frame the loss is not permanent — Smara lives on bodiless in every loving heart, and the tale is read at Kediri as the story of King Kamesvara ('Love's Slayer') himself.
summary.zh: 古爪哇詩中最哀傷的災變：為破濕婆之禪定，愛神蘇瑪羅（迦摩）射出花箭；震怒之神開第三眼，將其焚為灰燼，慾望自世界中死去。然詩之框架言其不滅——蘇瑪羅無形而存於每一顆相愛之心；諫義里宮廷將此篇讀作國王格梅斯瓦羅（『毀愛者』）自身之傳。

sensitivity.note: Court kakawin; the king's name-pun (Kamesvara) is the poem's hidden subject.

passages.text: To wake the meditating Shiva, the love-god Smara draws his bow of flowers and strikes the god with desire; Shiva's third eye opens and burns Smara where he stands, reducing the archer of hearts to ash. With Smara burned, desire dies from the world: couples grow cold, birds forget song, and heaven itself pines. The poem's consolation is bodiless survival — Smara lives in every heart that loves, invisible, and the burnt god's story is told at Kediri as the king's own name in disguise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Smaradahana (c. 12th c.); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kakawin Smaradahana; not verbatim.

title.en: Calon Arang, the Widow of Girah

region.zh: 東爪哇格拉鎮（艾爾朗加王國）

texts.period: Legend embedded in the Pararaton (Book of Kings); events set in the reign of Airlangga, c. 11th century CE

source.work: Pararaton (Book of Kings), the Calon Arang episode; Rangga Lawe and related Javanese MSS tradition

summary.en: The most feared witch of Javanese legend: the widow Calon Arang of Girah, who learned leyak magic and sickened the whole country with plague when no man would marry her daughter Ratna Manggali. King Airlangga, unable to defeat her by arms, sends the ascetic Mpu Barada in disguise; the widow is killed in her own ritual, and Girah is burnt to the ground.
summary.zh: 爪哇傳說中最令人畏懼的女巫：格拉鎮寡婦加隆·阿朗，習得黎雅克邪術；因無人肯娶其女拉特娜·芒加利，憤而以瘟疫荼毒全國。艾爾朗加王以兵不能克，乃遣苦修者姆普·巴拉達偽裝入鄉；寡婦死於自家祭儀，格拉全鎮付之一炬。

sensitivity.note: Pararaton episode; the leyak-witch figure remains part of living Balinese-Javanese folklore — treated as literature, not as accusation against living persons.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the Pararaton's Calon Arang episode; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Pararaton, the 'Book of Kings' of the Javanese tradition, embeds one of Java's great dark legends in the reign of King Airlangga (c. 1000-1040s CE): the tale of Calon Arang, the widow of Girah.

BEGINNING: THE WIDOW'S GRUDGE. In the village of Girah lives the widow Calon Arang, keeper of the black arts of the leyak — the headless flying witches of Javanese-Balinese fear. Her daughter Ratna Manggali is beautiful and good, but no man will marry into the witch's house; the stigma of the mother's magic blights the daughter's marriage prospects, and the widow's humiliation hardens into fury.

MIDDLE: THE PLAGUE OF GIRAH. To punish the country that spurned her daughter, Calon Arang unleashes her art: sickness spreads from Girah through the land of Airlangga's kingdom, people die in heaps, and the court's armies and prayers cannot stop the invisible attack. The king learns that the source is a woman and her grudge, not an enemy state.

END: THE COUNTER-WITCH. Unable to meet the widow by force, Airlangga turns to the ascetic Mpu Barada (with his disciple Mpu Bahula, given as a bridegroom to Ratna Manggali in some tellings, whose marriage opens the widow's house to the spy). Barada learns her arts under the guise of a pupil, then — at the climactic leyak ritual, when the widow and her followers begin their dance and transformation — he strikes her down, and the disease dies with her. Girah is burned to the ground so that nothing of the witch's town remains.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) polices the line between ritual power and witchcraft: the same arts that serve community become plague when privately held; (2) encodes gendered scapegoating, for the widow's rage begins in her daughter's blocked marriage — the court narrative sides with the state against the woman it cannot integrate; (3) provides the leyak cycle's charter (headless fliers, graveyards, night dances) as living folklore to this day; and (4) historicizes Airlangga's reign with a supernatural enemy worthy of the king who commissioned the Arjunawiwaha. The episode's afterlife is as significant as its plot. In Bali the widow's figure hardened into Rangda, the mask-queen of the leyak, and the Barong-Rangda drama re-enacts the plague and the counter-force in every village that keeps both masks; in Java the tale remained a literary episode of the Pararaton and its prose descendants, told as part of Airlangga's reign rather than as cult. The gendered logic of the story has drawn sustained scholarly attention: the court's counter-plot begins with a marriage — Mpu Bahula wed to Ratna Manggali — so that the daughter's blocked marriage, the cause of the plague, becomes the instrument of its ending. The witch's power is thus answered not by force but by the restoration of the alliance her grudge was protesting; the legend's own structure acknowledges what the widow wanted before it destroys her for wanting it.
narrative.zh: 《列王志》（Pararaton）在艾爾朗加王朝（約1000-1040年代）嵌入爪哇著名黑暗傳說：格拉鎮寡婦加隆·阿朗。她精通黎雅克邪術（無首飛行之巫）；其女拉特娜·芒加利美善而無人敢娶——母親之辱化為怨怒，乃以瘟疫荼毒全國，宮廷兵馬禱告俱不能止。王知病源乃一婦人之怨，遂遣苦修者姆普·巴拉達（一說其徒巴拉休拉詐娶其女以開其門）偽裝入鄉習其術；於最高潮之黎雅克祭舞之際擊殺之，瘟疫隨之而止；格拉全鎮焚燬以絕其跡。功能：劃分儀式之力與巫術之界、映照國家對無法整合之女性的替罪機制、為今日活態黎雅克傳說立憲章、並為艾爾朗加之治增一超自然之敵。

functions: Policing the boundary between licensed ritual power and illegitimate witchcraft (leyak)
Gendered scapegoat narrative: the widow's rage born from her daughter's blocked marriage
Charter of the leyak cycle (headless night fliers, graveyard dances) in living folklore
Supernatural enemy matched to Airlangga, the king of the Arjunawiwaha

passages.text: In Girah lives the widow Calon Arang, keeper of the leyak arts; her daughter Ratna Manggali is beautiful, but no man dares marry into the witch's house, and the widow's humiliation hardens into a grudge against the whole country. Sickness pours out of Girah into the land of King Airlangga; people die beyond the reach of arms and prayer, until the court understands that the plague is a woman's art turned loose.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pararaton's Calon Arang episode; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Pararaton episode; not verbatim.

passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pararaton episode; not verbatim.

title.en: Ken Arok Usurps Tumapel: The Murderer Who Founded a Dynasty
title.zh: 肯·阿洛克奪取杜馬佩爾：刺客立國

region.zh: 東爪哇杜馬佩爾（信訶沙里）

source.work: Pararaton (Book of Kings), the Ken Angrok narrative

summary.en: The Pararaton opens its dynastic history with regicide: the peasant-bandit Ken Arok murders the ruler of Tumapel (Tunggul Ametung) with the cursed kris Kyai Tanting Kembang, made by a smith whose wife he first dishonoured, marries the ruler's wife Ken Dedes — already pregnant and fated by prophecy to bear kings — and founds the Singhasari line from which Majapahit will descend. The chronicle does not disguise the crime; it makes the crime the price of the dynasty.
summary.zh: 《列王志》以弒君開其王朝史：草莽之徒肯·阿洛克以被咒之克利斯『丹婷·格孟』（先辱鑄師之妻而得）刺殺杜馬佩爾之主棟古爾·阿默通，娶其妻肯·德德絲——此女已孕，且預言注定誕下諸王——遂開信訶沙里王朝，日後馬卓帕希特即出其後。編年史不掩其罪；而以罪為王朝之代價。

sensitivity.note: Pararaton narrative; violence in the founding myth treated as literature.

passages.text: Ken Arok, a restless man of the village, serves the ruler of Tumapel while plotting his rise; the cursed kris Kyai Tanting Kembang, forged in blood and grudge, is set to kill for him until it finds its final victim in Tunggul Ametung, the ruler himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pararaton's Ken Angrok narrative; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ken Arok takes the widow Ken Dedes as his wife — already with child by the murdered ruler, and already marked by the prophecy that whoever possesses her bears kings. From that marriage the Singhasari dynasty is founded, and the chronicle's history of Java begins in a murder it never hides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pararaton narrative; not verbatim.

title.en: The Panji Cycle: The Lost Prince and Princess of Janggala
title.zh: 潘基傳說：章格拉失散的王儲與公主

region.zh: 東爪哇章格拉與諫義里

texts.period: Panji romance tradition, c. 13th-15th centuries; retold across the Malay world

source.archive: Javanese and Malay manuscript tradition (Panji cycle)
source.work: The Panji romances (Hikayat Panji tradition); East Javanese court romance

summary.en: Java's great romance: Panji, hero of Janggala, and his betrothed Sekar Taji (Chandra Kirana) of Daha are separated at the wedding by war and disguise; she wanders from court to court as a cooking-maid, a dancer, a queen under false names, while he searches under a string of aliases — until a ring, a dance, or a sleep-word reveals them to each other. The cycle's hundreds of tellings spread from Java into Malay, Thai, Burmese and Khmer court literature.
summary.zh: 爪哇之偉大傳奇：章格拉英雄潘基與達哈未婚妻瑟卡爾·達吉（查德拉·基拉娜）於婚禮之日因戰亂而失散；公主以假名流浪諸宮——或為庖娘、或為舞者、或為他國之王后；王子則以化名四處尋訪——直至一枚戒指、一支舞、或一句夢語令二人相認。此傳說百餘異本自爪哇遠播馬來、暹羅、緬甸與柬埔寨宮廷文學。

sensitivity.note: Court romance cycle; Southeast Asia's most widespread indigenous literary export.

passages.text: The wedding of the prince of Janggala and the princess of Daha is broken by war on the wedding morning itself; both vanish into exile under false names, she into servitude and queenship in foreign courts, he into a wandering of disguises that carries his fame from land to land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Panji romance tradition; not verbatim.

passages.text: Recognition comes by tokens rather than faces: the ring dropped in the bath, the dance learned in childhood, the sleep-talk that betrays a name. The cycle's countless versions end in the reunion of the two courts through the marriage of the two wanderers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Panji romance tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: Roro Jonggrang and the Thousand Temples in One Night
title.zh: 拉羅·鍾格朗與一夜千廟

texts.period: Javanese legend attached to the Prambanan temple (temple name recorded by Worsfold 1893); older oral tradition

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), ch. V, the temple of Loro-Jonggrang at Brambanan; Javanese oral legend

summary.en: To win the princess Roro Jonggrang, the ogre-prince Bandung Bondowoso must build a thousand temples in one night; the demons work at supernatural speed until the princess, fearing the dawn, orders her maids to pound rice and kindle fires — the cocks crow a false morning, the last temple lacks its idol, and the cheated prince turns the deceiver herself into stone: the Durga image in the northern cell of the temple still called Loro Jonggrang, 'the maiden of beautiful form.'
summary.zh: 為娶公主拉羅·鍾格朗，羅剎王子萬丹·邦多沃索須一夜建成千座神廟；群魔以妖速施工，公主懼黎明將至，密令宮女舂米生火——雄雞誤鳴而假晨至，最後一廟無像，被欺的王子將欺人者化為石：今日廟北殿中那尊杜爾迦像，仍名『拉羅·鍾格朗』——『美體之女』。

sensitivity.note: Best-known Central Javanese foundation legend; paraphrase of the oral cycle with the temple-name etymology from Worsfold.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the Javanese oral legend and the temple-name note in Worsfold (1893); paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The legend of Roro Jonggrang is Central Java's most famous etiological myth, fixed to the great Saivite temple of Prambanan — whose name, as Worsfold records, 'is simply the native name given to the particular Durga represented in the shrine, and means literally the Maiden with beautiful hips.'

BEGINNING: THE WAR AND THE WOOING. In the wars between the kingdoms of Pengging and Boko, the ogre-prince Bandung Bondowoso overthrows Pengging and demands the hand of Roro Jonggrang, daughter of the defeated king, as the price of peace. She cannot refuse and cannot accept; she sets an impossible bride-price: a thousand temples to be built in a single night.

MIDDLE: THE DEMONS BUILD. The prince commands his legions of ogres and spirits, and they work at supernatural speed — quarries open, walls rise, temples multiply through the dark hours toward the thousandth. As dawn approaches and the count nears its end, the princess acts: she orders the village women to pound rice in mortars and to kindle cooking fires on the eastern heights, so that the cocks, deceived by light and noise, crow before their time.

END: THE STONE MAIDEN. The demons scatter in terror at the false dawn; the work stops at nine hundred and ninety-nine temples, and the last one is left with no idol in its cell. Bandung Bondowoso, cheated, names the deception and curses his deceiver: Roro Jonggrang is turned to stone, seated forever in the shrine of the great temple — the image of Durga that the temple's own name commemorates. The thousandth temple, the people say, is the princess herself.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) explains the skyline of Prambanan and the Durga image's name; (2) encodes the cock-crow false-dawn motif (parallel to European rooster tales) as female resistance to a forced marriage; (3) fixes the moral ambiguity at the legend's heart — the princess lies, the prince curses, and both are caught in stone and story; and (4) binds modern Javanese identity to the monuments of the Hindu past through a story told in every school and wayang performance. The legend's geography is exact: the temple whose northern cell holds the stone Durga is the great Saivite complex at Prambanan, whose central temple still carries the name Loro Jonggrang, and the bandung of the ogre-prince's name is remembered in the plain to the west. Schoolchildren and dalangs alike tell the tale with the same beats — the impossible bride-price, the supernatural work-crew, the pounding mortars and fires on the eastern hills, the cock's false crow, the curse — and the wayang stages it as a standard lakon with the ogre-legions as shadow spectacle. The story's moral balance is deliberately uncomfortable: the princess lies to save her freedom, the prince curses her for a deception his own wager invited, and both are fixed forever in the landscape — one as stone, one as the name of the ruin where the stone sits. Javanese tellers rarely resolve the discomfort; the legend keeps it, as the temple keeps the image.
narrative.zh: 拉羅·鍾格朗傳說為中爪哇最著名釋源神話，附於普蘭巴南濕婆大神廟——沃斯福德記其廟名『即殿中所祀杜爾迦之土名，意為美體之女』。傳說：萬丹·邦多沃索王子破彭金國，索敗王之女拉羅·鍾格朗為妻；公主既不能拒又不能許，乃定天價彩禮：一夜建成千座神廟。王子驅群魔以妖速築廟，黎明將至、大功將成之際，公主密令村婦舂米、東嶺生火，雄雞受欺而提前報曉；群魔驚散，工程止於九百九十九廟，末廟無像。王子受騙，怒而將公主化為石，永坐大神廟北殿——即廟名所紀之杜爾迦像。村人云：第一千座廟，就是公主自己。功能：釋普蘭巴南廟群與杜爾迦像之名、以『假晨雞鳴』母題（可比歐洲雄雞傳說）寫女性對逼婚之抵抗、刻畫傳說核心的道德曖昧（公主設詐、王子施咒、二者皆困於石與故事）、並經由課堂與哇揚戲將爪哇認同繫於印度教古蹟。

functions: Etiology of the Prambanan skyline and the Durga image's name Loro Jonggrang
False-dawn cock-crow motif as female resistance to a forced marriage
Moral ambiguity: the lie that saves and the curse that punishes, both fixed in stone
Bridge between living Javanese identity and the Hindu monument past

variants.name: Borobudur bride-rejection telling (Scidmore 1897)
variants.text_tradition: Central Javanese temple legend recorded by Eliza Scidmore
variants.summary: The same pattern at Borobudur: a suitor builds the temple by night for the princess of Mendoet, who rejects the finished work as 'dead images' and leaves him to eternal meditation.

variants.name: Wayang lakon of Bandung Bondowoso
variants.summary: The legend is staged as a standard play, with the ogre-legions and the false dawn rendered in shadow.

primary_sources.work: Loro Jonggrang legend (Central Javanese oral tradition)
primary_sources.citation: Oral legend of Prambanan; temple-name etymology recorded in Worsfold, A Visit to Java, London 1893, ch. V.

secondary_sources.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java
secondary_sources.citation: Worsfold 1893, London: Cassell — ch. V on the temple of Loro-Jonggrang and the Durga image's name.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive full text of Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893)

passages.text: Bandung Bondowoso, prince of the ogres, demands the defeated king's daughter as the price of peace; Roro Jonggrang sets a bride-price meant to be impossible: a thousand temples built in one night. The ogre-legions build at supernatural speed through the dark hours; as the count nears a thousand, the princess orders the village women to pound rice and kindle fires on the eastern hills, and the cocks, deceived, crow before the true dawn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese oral legend of Roro Jonggrang; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese oral legend; not verbatim.

passages.text: The demons scatter at the false morning; the work stops short, the last temple lacks its idol, and the cheated prince turns the deceiver to stone — the Durga image in the shrine that bears her name, Loro Jonggrang, 'the maiden of beautiful form.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese oral legend, with the temple-name note from Worsfold (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Jaka Tarub and the Seven Bidadari: The Peeped Rice-Pot
title.zh: 加卡·塔魯布與七位天女：被偷看之飯鍋

region.en: Central Java (Mataram region, lake of the bidadari)
region.zh: 中爪哇（馬打藍地區，天女之湖）

texts.period: Javanese folk legend (oral tradition); recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.work: The legend of Jaka Tarub and Nawang Wulan (Javanese folktale cycle)

summary.en: The youth Jaka Tarub steals the shawl of the youngest of seven bathing bidadari and keeps her as his wife, Nawang Wulan — who cooks rice for the household from a single grain and forbids him ever to look into the pot. Of course he peeks: the rice turns to husks and chaff, the sky-robe is found, and Nawang Wulan rises back to heaven, leaving only her child — whom she may visit on a moonbeam, but never return to.
summary.zh: 青年加卡·塔魯布竊走七位浴水天女中最幼者之披肩，娶之為妻，名娜萬·吳蘭——她以一粒米為全家煮飯，並立禁令：永不可窺視飯鍋。他终究偷看：米化為糠殼，天衣被發現；娜萬·吳蘭復歸天上，只留下一個孩子——她可以沿月光下凡探望，卻永不能重返人間。

sensitivity.note: Celestial-wife cycle (star-wife type); the rice-pot taboo ties heaven to the harvest.

passages.text: Seven bidadari descend to bathe in the lake, hanging their shawls on the trees; Jaka Tarub takes the youngest's shawl, and the sky-maiden, grounded, accepts his house and his name for her — Nawang Wulan. She cooks with heaven's thrift — one grain fills the pot — and lays one prohibition: never look inside. Driven by doubt and slander, he peeks: the grain turns to husks, the hidden shawl is found, and Nawang Wulan, clothed again in light, rises to heaven, leaving the child below. Mother and child meet on the moonbeam she lowers at nights, but the marriage is over: the taboo broken is a marriage broken, and the boy grows up half of the sky, half of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese legend of Jaka Tarub; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese legend; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese legend; not verbatim.

title.en: Timun Mas, the Golden Cucumber Girl

region.zh: 中爪哇（西爾尼大娘之村）

source.work: The legend of Timun Mas (Javanese folktale cycle)

summary.en: The childless widow Mbok Sirni bargains with the green ogre Buto Ijo for a child and is given a cucumber seed: from the golden cucumber crawls the girl Timun Mas, with a payment falling due on her seventeenth birthday. Armed by a hermit with four packets — cucumber seeds, needles, salt and shrimp-paste — the girl flees the ogre, casting each gift behind her: a cucumber field to devour, a bamboo forest of needles, an ocean of salt, and a boiling sea of paste that swallows the giant whole.
summary.zh: 無子的西爾尼大娘與綠羅剎『布托·伊佐』訂約得子，得黃瓜一粒種——金瓜中爬出少女蒂蒙·瑪斯，而十七歲生日的贖金亦到期。隱士授她四包法物——黃瓜籽、鐵針、鹽、蝦醬——少女棄家而逃，邊逃邊擲：瓜田令巨魔飽食、針竹成林刺其足、鹽化大洋阻其路、蝦醬沸海將巨魔整個吞沒。

sensitivity.note: Giant-evader folktale; the four-throw escape is the Javanese analogue of magic-flight.

passages.text: Mbok Sirni's bargain brings a golden cucumber from whose rind crawls the girl Timun Mas — but the ogre Buto Ijo keeps the contract, and on her seventeenth birthday comes to collect the child for his meal. The hermit gives her four packets to throw as she flees: the seeds become a cucumber field the ogre must stop and devour; the needles a bamboo thorn-forest that stings his feet; the salt an ocean; and the shrimp-paste a boiling mud-sea in which the giant sinks and is swallowed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese legend of Timun Mas; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese legend; not verbatim.

title.en: Keong Emas: The Princess in the Golden Snail

region.en: Daha and Kediri, East Java (Panji-cycle setting)
region.zh: 東爪哇達哈與諫義里（潘基傳說背景）

texts.period: Javanese folk romance (oral tradition, Panji cycle offshoot)

source.work: The legend of Keong Emas (Javanese folktale, Panji-cycle offshoot)

summary.en: The rejected suitor king of AntanginJagar, cursed and transformed, pays out his rage in magic: Princess Sekar Taji, lost on the wedding morning, is turned into a golden snail and cast into a river; a fisher-widow nets the snail and keeps it as a treasure, for the snail secretly cooks and cleans her hut. When the widow spies on the gift, the woman inside is caught — and the long recognition begins that will carry the princess back to her name, her ring, and her waiting Panji.
summary.zh: 安坦金賈加爾的被拒求婚者懷怨弄法：婚晨走失的瑟卡爾·達吉公主被化為金螺、拋入河中；漁婦撒網得螺，視為寶物收藏——螺竟暗自為她煮飯掃屋。漁婦窺破其秘，螺中人現形——漫長的相認之旅由此開始，公主終將尋回自己的名字、戒指，以及等待她的潘基。

sensitivity.note: Panji-cycle offshoot; the animal-bride motif attached to Java's great romance.

passages.text: Denied at the wedding morning, the rejected king works his grudge into magic: Sekar Taji is transformed into a golden snail and thrown into the river, her name lost with her shape. A fisher-widow nets the shining snail and keeps it caged as treasure; unknown to her, the woman inside slips out by night to cook and sweep the hut. Discovered at last, the princess tells her name and story, and the recognition sets the whole Panji cycle's search back on its road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Keong Emas legend; not verbatim.

title.en: The Hill of Tidar: The Nail That Fastens Java to the Earth
title.zh: 蒂達爾丘：把爪哇釘在大地上的釘子

region.en: Hill of Tidar, Magelang, Central Java
region.zh: 中爪哇馬格朗蒂達爾丘

texts.period: Javanese sacred-geography tradition, recorded in Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897)

source.work: Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), the hill of Tidar

summary.en: At the base of Java's central volcano trio, Soembung — 'the very centre of Java' — native legends cling to the little hill of Tidar: it is the 'spike of the universe,' the nail which fastens the lovely island to the face of the earth. A whole island's stability hangs on one small green hill.
summary.zh: 爪哇中央三峰環峙之處，松邦峰——『爪哇之正中』——山腳的小丘蒂達爾承載著本地傳說：它是『宇宙之釘』，將這可愛的島嶼釘牢在大地之上。整座島的安穩，繫於一座小小的青山。

sensitivity.note: Sacred-geography note; Tidar hill is also a modern military academy site.

passages.text: Soembung is the very center of Java, and native legends cling to the little hill of Tidar at its base — the 'spike of the universe,' the nail which fastens the lovely island to the face of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Papandayan the Forge: The Chained Giants in the Mountain
title.zh: 帕潘達揚『鍛爐』：山中的鎖鏈巨人

region.zh: 西爪哇加魯特帕潘達揚火山

texts.period: Sundanese mountain legend recorded in Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897)

source.work: Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), Garoet and Papandayang

summary.en: Inside the Papandayan crater the pools of sulphur boil like vats of molten gold, scattering golden drops, and steam jets roar from the quaking solfatara; the natives named the mountain 'The Forge,' and their legends hear chained giants groaning inside the mountain — the underworld's prisoners heard in the rumblings of the volcano.
summary.zh: 帕潘達揚火山口內，硫磺池如熔金之釜沸騰四濺；地汽嘶吼、大地顫動。土人名此山為『鍛爐』，傳說中聽見鎖鏈之巨人在山中呻吟——那是冥界囚徒在火山轟鳴裏的聲音。

sensitivity.note: Volcano-legend; the forge metaphor is recorded traveller ethnography.

passages.text: The kawa, or crater, is a bowl deep sunk in rocky walls, with pools of liquid sulphur boiling like vats of purest molten gold; from the rumblings and strange underground noises one can understand the native legends of chained giants groaning inside of the mountain, and their name for Papandayang, 'The Forge.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897); not verbatim.

title.en: The Prince of Mendoet: A Temple Built in Ten Days, a Family in Stone
title.zh: 門多特王儲：十日建廟，闔家化石

region.en: Mendoet temple, near Borobudur, Central Java
region.zh: 中爪哇婆羅浮屠附近門多特廟

texts.period: Central Javanese temple legend recorded in Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897)

source.work: Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), Boro Boedor and Mendoet

summary.en: The two-year-old daughter of Prince Dewa Kosoumi is stolen by a revengeful courtier; twelve years later the broken-hearted prince meets and marries the most beautiful girl he has ever seen — his own child. When the truth is told, the priests rule that no forgiveness is possible unless he builds a great temple in ten days; the kingdom's artists finish Borobudur-like marvel within the term, but one statue is missing. The gods turn the prince, the mother, and the child to stone: they sit in the cell at Mendoet as proof of the tale for all time.
summary.zh: 德瓦·科蘇米王儲兩歲之女被復仇的廷臣偷走；十二年後，心碎的王儲遇見並娶了平生所見最美的少女——竟是自己的女兒。真相揭穿，祭司裁定：唯有十日之內建成大神廟方可赦免；全國工匠瘋狂趕工如期而成——卻恰好缺一尊像。神遂將王儲、其妻、其子化為石：三人永坐門多特廟中之室，為此故事作萬世之證。

sensitivity.note: Temple legend; incest-expiation narrative treated as recorded folklore.

passages.text: The little daughter of the great Prince Dewa Kosoumi is stolen by a revengeful courtier; twelve years later the prince, wandering the country in search of her, meets and marries the most beautiful young girl he has ever seen. The revengeful courtier of years before tells the prince that his beautiful wife is his own daughter; the priests assure the prince that no forgiveness is possible, and that his only expiation lies in a walled cell and prayer — unless within ten days he can construct a Boro Boedor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), Boro Boedor and Mendoet; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Scidmore (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the artists and workmen of the kingdom, working with zeal and frenzy to save their ruler, complete the temple within the fixed time — but the pile lacks just one statue of the full number required. Prayers and appeals are useless: the gods turn the prince, the mother, and the child to stone, and they sit in the cell at Mendoet as proof of the tale for all time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore (1897); not verbatim.

title.en: 'These Images Are Dead': The Princess Who Rejected Borobudur
title.zh: 『這些像都是死的』：拒絕婆羅浮屠的公主

texts.period: Central Javanese temple legend recorded in Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897)

source.work: Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), Boro Boedor and Mendoet

summary.en: In the hypnotic hours at Borobudur one can best believe the tradition that the temple rose in a night at miraculous bidding, built by the son of the Prince of Borobudur as the condition of marrying the daughter of the Prince of Mendoet. Every detail rigidly prescribed, the work is finished; the princess inspects the miles of carvings and hundreds of statues and says coldly: 'Without doubt these images are beautiful, but they are dead. I can no more love you than they can love you' — and leaves her lover to brood in eternal meditation on the temple walls.
summary.zh: 在婆羅浮屠催眠般的午後，人們最易相信那傳統：此廟乃一夜之間奉神諭而起，由婆羅浮屠王子所建，以此為迎娶門多特公主之條件。工程如期而成，公主巡視綿延的浮雕與成百的雕像，冷然道：『無疑這些像很美，但它們是死的。我愛不上你，正如它們愛不上你。』——她轉身離去，留下她的追求者在廟牆上永恆地冥想。

sensitivity.note: Bride-rejection temple legend; the Javanese analogue of the Roro Jonggrang cycle applied to Borobudur.

passages.text: The tradition says the temple rose in a night at miraculous bidding, built by the son of the Prince of Boro Boedor as a condition to his receiving the daughter of the Prince of Mendoet for a wife; the suitor was to build it within a given time, and every detail was rigidly prescribed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The princess came with her father to inspect the great work — miles of bas-reliefs, hundreds of statues fresh from the chisel. 'Without doubt these images are beautiful,' she said coldly, 'but they are dead. I can no more love you than they can love you'; and she turned and left her lover to brood in eternal sorrow and meditation upon that puzzle of all the centuries — the Eternal Feminine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore (1897); not verbatim.
